items.name: Proton pump inhibitors
hx: Reversibly block parietal-cell H₂ receptors
That's how famotidine works; PPIs irreversibly block the proton pump.
Neutralise acid already secreted into the stomach
That's antacids; PPIs stop acid being secreted.
Block gastrin release from G cells
Gastrin actually rises on PPIs; they block the final acid pump.
items.sewhy: Less acid allows C. difficile spores to survive and reduces absorption of B12, magnesium and calcium (fractures); hyponatraemia is a less common effect.

ci.why: Less gastric acid lets spores survive
x: More gastric acid damages the colon lining
PPIs reduce acid, which lets spores survive the stomach.
PPIs kill normal gut flora directly
They aren't antibiotics; less acid lets spores through.
PPIs stop C. difficile toxin being cleared in bile
No; acid suppression lets spores survive.
Raises clopidogrel levels → bleeding; use omeprazole
Omeprazole lowers activation (CYP2C19); lansoprazole is preferred.
Blocks clopidogrel absorption; separate by 4 hours
It's metabolic (CYP2C19), so spacing doesn't help; switch PPI.
Increases GI bleeding; stop the PPI
PPIs protect against GI bleeding; the problem is less clopidogrel activation.
Long-term use ↑ vitamin D toxicity
No; less acid reduces calcium absorption, raising fracture risk.
Short-term use ↑ calcium levels
The concern is long-term fracture risk.
Long-term use ↑ osteonecrosis of the jaw
Jaw osteonecrosis is a bisphosphonate risk; PPIs raise fracture risk.

items.name: Loperamide
items.how: Peripheral μ-opioid agonist: slows gut motility, ↑ anal tone; doesn't cross the BBB
hx: Central μ-opioid agonist: slows gut motility, ↓ anal tone; crosses the BBB
It acts on gut μ receptors and doesn't reach the brain at normal doses.
Peripheral κ-opioid antagonist: speeds gut motility, ↓ anal tone
It's a μ-opioid agonist that slows motility.
Binds bile acids in the gut: firms stool, ↑ anal tone
That's colestyramine; loperamide is a peripheral μ-opioid agonist.
items.sewhy: As a gut μ-opioid agonist it slows transit (constipation, cramps, bloating); in large overdoses it blocks cardiac channels, causing arrhythmias.

ci.why: Keeps invasive bacteria and toxins in the gut
x: Masks the fever, delaying diagnosis
It doesn't affect fever; slowing the gut traps invasive bacteria and toxins.
Kills protective gut flora
It's not antibacterial; it keeps pathogens in the gut.
Causes rebound diarrhoea when stopped
Not the reason; it traps invasive bacteria and toxins.
Risk of a perforated ulcer
The danger is toxic megacolon.
Risk of C. difficile resistance
Not resistance; toxic megacolon.
Risk of dehydration
It reduces fluid loss; the danger is toxic megacolon.
Can precipitate a relapse months later
The danger is immediate: toxic megacolon.
Can precipitate small-bowel obstruction
In acute colitis the danger is toxic megacolon.
Can precipitate colorectal cancer
No; it can precipitate toxic megacolon.

items.name: Bulk-forming laxatives
items.how: Retain water → bulkier stool → stimulates peristalsis
hx: Coat the stool with oil → easier passage, no change in bulk
That's a lubricant (liquid paraffin); ispaghula holds water and adds bulk.
Absorb water from stool → firmer stool → slower transit
They retain water in the stool, making it bulkier and softer.
Ferment to gas → distend the colon → trigger the defecation reflex
Gas is a side effect, not the mechanism; they add bulk.
se: Obstruction if taken without enough fluid
items.sewhy: Fibre is fermented by gut bacteria (gas, bloating) and swells with water, so without enough fluid it can cause obstruction.

x: Speeds transit past the blockage
It can't pass; it adds bulk behind it.
Causes rebound constipation
No; it adds bulk behind the blockage.
Irritates the bowel wall → ischaemia
Not irritation; bulk builds up behind the blockage.
Interacts with opioids to cause sedation
No interaction; bulk can't overcome slowed motility.
Speeds opioid absorption
No; they just don't overcome reduced motility.
Triggers opioid withdrawal
No; they're simply ineffective against an opioid-slowed gut.

items.name: Osmotic laxatives
items.how: Hold water in the bowel lumen by osmosis
hx: Draw water out of the bowel lumen into the blood
They hold water in the lumen, softening stool.
Block water reabsorption channels (aquaporins) in the colon
They work by osmosis, not by blocking channels.
Neutralise colonic acid to soften stool
They hold water osmotically.
items.sewhy: Unabsorbed sugars or polymers hold water in the bowel; bacteria ferment lactulose (gas), and excess water loss can disturb electrolytes.

x: Reduces bowel blood flow by osmosis
The concern is fluid and pressure building behind the blockage.
Causes electrolyte loss → ileus
Not the main reason; it raises pressure behind the obstruction.
Speeds transit through the blockage
It can't pass; pressure builds behind it.

ci.c: Severe inflammatory bowel disease / toxic megacolon
x: Risk of dehydration
The danger is perforating a fragile colon.
Risk of fistula
Perforation is the risk.
Risk of IBD relapse
Not relapse; perforation.

items.name: Stimulant laxatives
items.how: Stimulate enteric nerves → ↑ colonic motility and secretion
hx: Block enteric nerves → ↓ colonic water absorption
They stimulate enteric nerves, increasing motility and secretion.
Stimulate colonic μ-opioid receptors → ↑ motility
μ-opioid stimulation slows the gut; they act on enteric nerves.
Stimulate gastric acid → a faster gastrocolic reflex
No; they stimulate colonic enteric nerves.
items.sewhy: They stimulate colonic nerves and muscle (cramps, diarrhoea); chronic overuse causes potassium loss.

ci.why: Forceful peristalsis against a blockage → perforation
x: Gentle peristalsis can't pass the blockage, so no effect
Stimulants drive forceful peristalsis, risking perforation.
Electrolyte loss causes paralytic ileus
Not the reason; forceful contraction against a blockage can perforate.
The bowel wall absorbs the drug → toxicity
No; it's forceful peristalsis against a blockage.
Risk of colonic melanosis
Melanosis coli is harmless pigmentation; the danger is perforation.
Risk of rebound constipation
The danger is perforation.
Risk of IBD relapse
Not relapse; perforation.

items.name: Metoclopramide
hx: D2 agonist (CTZ) with antimotility effect
It blocks D2 and speeds gastric emptying.
NK1 antagonist (brainstem) with antisecretory effect
That's aprepitant-like; metoclopramide blocks D2 and is prokinetic.
D2 antagonist (basal ganglia only) with sedative effect
Its antiemetic effect is at the CTZ, and it speeds gut emptying.
items.sewhy: Blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the basal ganglia causes dystonia (especially in young women) and tardive dyskinesia with long use, and in the pituitary raises prolactin; hence the 5-day limit.

x: Antimotility effect hides the blockage
It's prokinetic, pushing against the blockage.
Causes hypokalaemia → ileus
Not the reason; it drives peristalsis against the blockage.
D2 blockade raises gut secretions → perforation
The issue is its prokinetic drive.

ci.why: D2 blockade worsens parkinsonism; use domperidone
x: D2 stimulation worsens dyskinesia; use haloperidol
It blocks D2 centrally (and haloperidol is worse); domperidone doesn't cross the BBB.
Interferes with levodopa absorption; use ondansetron
The issue is central D2 blockade; domperidone is the usual choice.
Causes hypotension with levodopa; use cyclizine
The issue is central D2 blockade worsening parkinsonism.
Can trigger a hypoglycaemic crisis
It can release catecholamines, causing a hypertensive crisis.
Can trigger an adrenal crisis
Not adrenal insufficiency; a catecholamine surge.
Can trigger a thyroid storm
No; it can cause a hypertensive crisis.

items.name: Ondansetron
hx: 5-HT4 agonist (gut wall) with prokinetic effect
It blocks 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and the CTZ.
5-HT3 agonist (vomiting centre and cortex)
It's an antagonist, acting on vagal afferents and the CTZ.
Muscarinic antagonist (vestibular nuclei)
That's hyoscine's motion-sickness action; ondansetron blocks 5-HT3.
items.sewhy: Blocking 5-HT3 receptors in the gut slows transit (constipation) and causes headache; it can prolong QT.

x: QT shortening → VF
It prolongs QT.
Further PR prolongation → heart block
The concern is QT prolongation and torsades.
Further QT prolongation → complete heart block
QT prolongation leads to torsades, not heart block.
Small ↑ risk of limb reduction defects
The signal was a small rise in cleft lip/palate.
Large ↑ risk of miscarriage
No; there's a small orofacial cleft signal.
Small ↑ risk of hyperemesis
It treats hyperemesis; the concern is a small rise in clefts.

items.name: Cyclizine

uses.t: Nausea and vomiting, vestibular and post-op

items.how: H1 antihistamine (also antimuscarinic) acting on the vomiting centre
hx: H2 antihistamine (also antiemetic) acting on the stomach
It's an H1 antihistamine acting centrally.
Dopamine antagonist (also antihistamine) acting on the gut wall
It's an H1 antihistamine with antimuscarinic effects.
H1 agonist (also cholinergic) acting on the vestibular nuclei
It blocks H1 (and muscarinic) receptors.
items.sewhy: As an antihistamine with antimuscarinic effects it causes drowsiness, dry mouth, urinary retention and tachycardia.

x: Causes fluid retention
The concern is raised heart rate and afterload.
Lowers heart rate and contractility
It raises heart rate and afterload.
Interacts with diuretics → hypokalaemia
No; it raises heart rate and afterload.
Antihistamine sedation
The problem is its antimuscarinic action.
Cholinergic effects
It's anticholinergic (antimuscarinic).
Dopamine blockade
Not dopamine; antimuscarinic effects.

items.name: Mesalazine (5-ASA)
items.how: Topical anti-inflammatory in the colon (↓ prostaglandins, leukotrienes, NF-κB)
hx: Systemic immunosuppressant (↓ T-cell proliferation)
It acts topically on the colonic lining.
Topical antibacterial in the colon (kills invasive bacteria)
It's anti-inflammatory, not antibacterial.
Topical steroid in the colon (glucocorticoid receptors)
It's an aminosalicylate, not a steroid.
items.sewhy: Most adverse effects are idiosyncratic: interstitial nephritis (monitor renal function), blood dyscrasias (report unexplained bleeding or sore throat) and pancreatitis.

x: Can cause kidney stones
The renal risk is interstitial nephritis.
Can cause hyperkalaemia
Not the reason; interstitial nephritis.
Can cause renal artery stenosis
No; interstitial nephritis.
Structurally related to penicillin
Mesalazine is a salicylate, like aspirin.
Releases histamine directly
Not the reason; it's a salicylate.
Contains a sulfa group
That's sulfasalazine; mesalazine is related to aspirin.

items.name: Thiopurines
hx: Pyrimidine antimetabolite → ↓ neutrophil production
They're purine analogues that stop lymphocytes proliferating.
Calcineurin inhibitor → ↓ IL-2 and T-cell activation
That's ciclosporin and tacrolimus; thiopurines block purine synthesis.
Monoclonal antibody → depletes B lymphocytes
That's rituximab; thiopurines are oral purine antimetabolites.
items.sewhy: Thiopurines block purine synthesis in dividing cells, so they suppress the marrow and immunity (infections, skin cancer, lymphoma); they can also damage the liver and pancreas. Low TPMT increases toxicity.

ci.why: Can't metabolise the drug → severe marrow failure; check TPMT first
x: Can't activate the drug → no effect; check TPMT after a month
Without TPMT, toxic metabolites build up → marrow failure.
Can't excrete the drug → kidney failure; check eGFR first
The issue is marrow toxicity from absent TPMT.
Can't metabolise the drug → severe pancreatitis; check amylase first
Pancreatitis is a side effect unrelated to TPMT; the risk is marrow failure.

ci.why: Xanthine oxidase is blocked → toxic thiopurine levels
x: TPMT is induced → thiopurines stop working
Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, so thiopurine levels rise.
Urate crystals form in the marrow
No; blocking xanthine oxidase raises thiopurine levels.
Xanthine oxidase is activated → low thiopurine levels
It's inhibited, so levels rise to toxic.

ci.why: Immunosuppressed patients can be infected by the vaccine strain
x: The vaccine lowers thiopurine levels
No interaction; the live strain can infect an immunosuppressed host.
Vaccines trigger a flare of IBD
Not the concern; the vaccine strain can cause infection.
Vaccine antibodies attack the bone marrow
No; the live strain can cause disease.

items.name: Anti-TNF biologics
hx: Monoclonal antibodies that neutralise IL-6
That's tocilizumab; infliximab and adalimumab target TNF-α.
Small molecules that block JAK signalling
That's tofacitinib; these are anti-TNF antibodies.
Recombinant TNF-α that desensitises its receptor
They neutralise TNF-α rather than replace it.
items.sewhy: TNF holds granulomas together and fights infection, so blocking it reactivates latent TB and raises serious infection risk; immune dysregulation can cause demyelination and lupus-like syndromes.

x: TNF triggers granuloma breakdown → spread
TNF maintains granulomas; blocking it lets TB reactivate.
The antibody binds TB drugs and inactivates them
No interaction; losing TNF lets granulomas fall apart.
TB bacteria make TNF that neutralises the drug
No; TNF holds granulomas together.
Raises fever dangerously
It removes a key immune defence.
Causes bacterial resistance
Not resistance; it removes a key defence.
Triggers a cytokine storm
It blocks a cytokine; the issue is losing that defence.
Causes heart block
The concern is worsening heart failure.
Causes pericarditis
No; it worsens heart failure.
Raises potassium
No; trials showed worsening heart failure.
Can trigger optic nerve infection
The concern is demyelination.
Can trigger PML in most patients
PML is natalizumab's risk; anti-TNF can worsen demyelination.
Can block MS treatments
No interaction; it can worsen demyelination.
Viral resistance
The risk is hepatitis B reactivation.
Drug hepatotoxicity alone
The concern is hep B reactivating.
Vaccine failure
Not the reason; viral reactivation.

items.name: Hyoscine butylbromide
items.how: Antimuscarinic: relaxes GI smooth muscle; doesn't cross the BBB
hx: Antimuscarinic: relaxes GI smooth muscle; crosses the BBB to stop nausea
Butylbromide is quaternary, so it doesn't reach the brain (unlike hyoscine hydrobromide).
Muscarinic agonist: contracts GI smooth muscle; doesn't cross the BBB
It blocks muscarinic receptors, relaxing gut muscle.
Nicotinic antagonist: paralyses gut skeletal muscle; doesn't cross the BBB
The gut wall is smooth muscle; it's antimuscarinic.
items.sewhy: It blocks muscarinic receptors, so it causes dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention and blurred vision (it doesn't cross the blood–brain barrier, so no sedation).

x: Pupil constriction blocks drainage
Antimuscarinics dilate the pupil.
Raised aqueous production
Not production; the dilated pupil blocks drainage.
Raised venous pressure in the eye
No; pupil dilation blocks drainage.
Causes a cholinergic crisis
It's anticholinergic; it worsens weakness.
Blocks pyridostigmine absorption
Not absorption; its antimuscarinic action worsens weakness.
Triggers thymoma growth
No; it worsens weakness.

ci.c: Mechanical bowel obstruction or toxic megacolon
x: Speeds motility → perforation at the blockage
It stops motility, letting the bowel dilate.
Raises gut secretions → dilatation
It reduces secretions; the problem is stopped motility.
Constricts mesenteric vessels → bowel ischaemia
No vascular effect; stopped motility lets the bowel dilate.

items.name: Misoprostol
items.how: Prostaglandin E1 analogue: protects gastric mucosa; contracts the uterus
hx: Prostaglandin E1 antagonist: reduces gastric acid; relaxes the uterus
It mimics PGE1, so it contracts the uterus.
H₂ antagonist: reduces gastric acid; no uterine effect
It's a prostaglandin analogue with strong uterine effects.
Oxytocin analogue: protects the gastric mucosa; contracts the uterus
It's a prostaglandin E1 analogue, not oxytocin.
items.sewhy: As a prostaglandin E1 analogue it stimulates gut motility (diarrhoea, cramps) and uterine contraction (cramps, bleeding).

x: Uterine relaxation → bleeding
It contracts the uterus, causing miscarriage.
Fetal gastric ulcers → bleeding
No; uterine contractions cause miscarriage.
Maternal hypertension → pre-eclampsia
No; it causes uterine contractions.

items.name: Orlistat
items.how: Inhibits pancreatic lipase → ~30% less fat absorbed
hx: Inhibits pancreatic amylase → ~30% less carbohydrate absorbed
It inhibits lipase, reducing fat absorption.
Suppresses appetite centrally → ~30% fewer calories eaten
It acts in the gut lumen, not the brain.
Blocks bile acid reabsorption → ~30% less cholesterol absorbed
That's colestyramine-like; orlistat blocks lipase.
items.sewhy: Blocking pancreatic lipase leaves fat undigested in the gut (oily stools, urgency) and reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

x: Causes coeliac antibodies to form
No; it worsens fat malabsorption.
Blocks gluten digestion
No; it worsens existing malabsorption.
Speeds weight gain
No; it worsens malabsorption and deficiencies.
Bile flow is already excessive
In cholestasis bile flow is reduced.
Raises bilirubin directly
Not the reason; bile flow is already impaired.
Causes gallstones in everyone
No; bile flow is already impaired.
